extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of literature, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Aristotle's Poetics lays out classical, prescriptive principles for composing and judging poetry (especially tragedy, epic, and comedy), focusing on imitation, plot structure, and the constituent parts of dramatic works. It is a guide for constructing effective plots, characters, diction, music, and spectacle to achieve the proper emotional and aesthetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as Imitation (Mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry and Tragedy, as also Comedy, Dithyrambic poetry, and most flute-playing and lyre-playing, are all, viewed as a whole, modes of imitation. They differ in three points; they imitate (a) different objects, (b) by different means, (c) differently (i.e. different manner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats imitation as the defining principle of poetic arts. The means (rhythm, language, harmony), the objects (kinds of persons/actions), and the manner (narrative, assumed character, fully enacted drama) distinguish genres. Examples: dance imitates by rhythm, flute by rhythm+melody, language-only imitations include dialogues and mimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is 'the imitation of an action that is serious and also, as having magnitude, complete in itself; in language with pleasurable accessories, each kind brought in separately in the parts of the work; in a dramatic, not in a narrative form; with incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key required features: seriousness, completeness (unity), magnitude, suitable language with 'pleasurable accessories' (rhythm, harmony/song), dramatic enactment (not mere narration), and incidents designed to arouse pity and fear culminating in catharsis. When judging or composing a tragedy, test for each of these components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Constituent Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are six parts consequently of every tragedy ... viz. a Fable or Plot, Characters, Diction, Thought, Spectacle and Melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to evaluate or construct tragedy. Aristotle notes two arise from means (Diction, Melody), one from manner (Spectacle), and three from objects/motivation (Plot, Character, Thought). Each part should be present and correctly ordered, though their relative importance differs (Plot is most important).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Fable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important of the six is the combination of the incidents of the story. Tragedy is essentially an imitation not of persons but of action and life ... the action in it, i.e. its Fable or Plot, that is the end and purpose of the tragedy; and the end is everywhere the chief thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plots by their internal logic and capacity to generate tragic effect: the Plot (sequence of incidents) should constitute the primary organizing principle. A play with inferior diction or character can still succeed if the Plot is strong; conversely, fine speeches alone cannot produce true tragedy without a coherent Plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, Completeness, and Magnitude of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy ... complete in itself; as having magnitude. The Plot should have a beginning, a middle and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-formed plot must be whole (complete), of appropriate scope (magnitude), and unified (each part contributes to the one action). The beginning is that which does not necessarily follow anything prior; the end is that which itself naturally follows from what precedes. Avoid irrelevant episodes; each incident should subserve the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity (Causal Coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle recommends that sequences of events should be 'either necessary or probable' and 'appear to happen because of one another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events must cohere causally—do not rely on arbitrary coincidences or implausible twists. Even if not strictly necessary, incidents should be probable given characters and prior events so the plot feels convincing and inevitable in hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plots; Role of Peripeteia and Anagnorisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle assumes that Discovery (Anagnorisis) and Peripety (Reversal of Fortune) are normally present in any tragedy that really has a plot; the most powerful elements of attraction in Tragedy, the Peripeties and Discoveries, are parts of the Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'complex' plots (which include recognition and reversal) from 'simple' ones. Use Anagnorisis and Peripeteia strategically to heighten pity/fear and produce catharsis; their combination is particularly effective. Judge whether these moments arise organically from the plot's causal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (Purgation of Pity and Fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions. (katharsis: 'purification' or 'purgation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intended effect of tragedy is to elicit and then purge pity and fear in the audience. When evaluating, ask whether the play genuinely arouses these emotions and whether their resolution provides a cleansing or transformative effect. Aristotle links katharsis to ritual/purification origins of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (Tragic Error or Flaw)
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical tragic hero is one who falls from high state or fame, not through vice or depravity, but by some great hamartia. Hamartia means originally a 'bad shot' or 'error', but is currently used for 'offence' or 'sin'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist's downfall should stem from an error of judgment or fate-linked mistake rather than simple moral depravity. When composing or assessing a tragic figure, look for a plausible, often intellectual or situational error that triggers reversal rather than mere villainy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: Appropriateness and Role in Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is what makes us ascribe certain moral qualities to the agents; Character gives us qualities, but it is in our actions—what we do—that we are happy or the reverse ... the agents represented must be either above our own level of goodness, or beneath it, or just such as we are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be consistent and appropriate to the plot and genre (tragedy tends to present personages better than ourselves; comedy worse). Characters serve action: they exist to make the action plausible and necessary. Evaluate whether characters' traits naturally produce their choices and the resulting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Language) and Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'Diction' I mean merely this, the composition of the verses; and by 'Thought' is shown in all they say when proving a particular point or, it may be, enunciating a general truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction concerns the verbal expression—meter, style, phrasing—appropriate to characters and effects. Thought concerns the arguments, beliefs, and reasoning expressed. Both should be judged for clarity, appropriateness, and how well they support the plot and elicit the intended emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (Music) and Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (stage-appearance of the actors) must be some part of the whole; and Melody ... is one of the means of imitation. Spectacle, Melody and Diction are the means by which imitation is effected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melody (song, musical elements) should be integrated with the dramatic parts; Spectacle (scenery, visual effects) is a component but has less to do with the poet's art (it appeals to senses). Use both to enhance but not substitute for Plot and Character; spectacle must serve the whole, not distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of Subject Matter and 'Great Way of Living'
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle lays his greatest stress ... on the need for Unity in the work of art ... and next, on the demand that great art must have for its subject the great way of living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects of sufficient dignity and seriousness for tragedy (matters of 'high life' or 'magnitudinous' concerns). Evaluate whether the material is worthy of the genre's aims and whether smaller or trivial subjects are ill-suited to tragic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific Characteristics (Epic and Comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from Tragedy ... (1) in that it is in one kind of verse and in narrative form; and (2) in its length ... Comedy is an imitation of men worse than the average; the Ridiculous may be defined as a mistake or deformity not productive of pain or harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing/judging epics: expect narrative hexameter form, larger temporal scope, and inclusion of elements found in tragedy but with differences in mode. For comedy: evaluate treatment of the ridiculous (not harmful), use of masks, fable/plot invention, and whether the ridicule is harmless and focused on the comic defect rather than moral harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, Development, and 'Natural Form' of Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of art grow and develop, but not indefinitely; they develop until they 'attain their natural form'; also the rule that each form of art should produce 'not every sort of pleasure but its proper pleasure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a work against the mature norms of its form: has the genre reached its natural structure (e.g., number of actors, use of chorus, meters)? Consider whether the work provides the 'proper pleasure' of its kind (e.g., tragic catharsis, comic laughter) rather than mixing incompatible pleasures incoherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Meter and Delivery for Spoken Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic, we know, is the most speakable of metres, as is shown by the fact that we very often fall into it in conversation, whereas we rarely talk hexameters, and only when we depart from the speaking tone of voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose meters that suit the spoken/dramatic tone: conversational parts benefit from iambic metres, elevated or narrative parts may suit hexameter. Meter affects perceived naturalness and the audience's reception; match meter to purpose and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and Proper Use of the Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus ... should be an integral part of the play, ... it should be regarded as one of the actors (though Aristotle notes later-day misunderstandings when chorus technique was lost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus to contribute to the unity of the action and the emotional effect; it should form part of the whole rather than be an irrelevant appendage. Beware treating the chorus merely as spectacle or expository device disconnected from the plot's development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Irrelevancies; Parts Should Subserve Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity in the work of art, the need that each part should subserve the whole, while irrelevancies, however brilliant in themselves, should be cast away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing or evaluating, remove brilliant but irrelevant passages, characters, or episodes that do not advance the single action or the work's purpose. Favor economy and unity over digressive display.
